A cautious modern component gloss is that 乱 is compatible with a disorderly or unruly quality, while 暴 is compatible with rough, forceful, or violent behavior. This is an interpretation from the characters’ independently listed Japanese meanings, not a documented analysis of the compound’s word formation.

The 亂 character note describes a character history involving disordered thread ends and arranging them, then use for disorder. This is a character-history account and does not establish the historical derivation of Japanese 乱暴.

The opened sources differ in certainty about 暴’s graphic history: 字通 presents an account involving exposed animal remains, whereas the Taishukan reference says the formation is unclear and presents that account as one among multiple theories. guides.explanation_en: 愛 means love or affection: caring attachment toward a person or thing. It can describe love within close relationships, including family love.
見る is the basic verb for seeing or looking at something. The thing seen is usually marked by を; context shows whether the focus is simply perceiving it or directing one’s gaze toward it.
目を覚ます frames waking as “awakening the eyes”: を marks 目 as the object of 覚ます, “to awaken.” As an expression, it means that a person wakes up or regains consciousness.

parts.contribution_en: “Eyes,” the object being awakened in the expression.
Marks 目 as the object of 覚ます.
“To awaken”; here, it describes awakening the eyes as the person becomes awake.

guides.explanation_en: いびきをかく is the ordinary expression for “to snore.” いびき names the snoring sound, を marks it as what is produced, and かく is conventionally used with this noun to mean making that sound.

parts.contribution_en: The snoring sound, or snoring.
Marks いびき as the object of かく.
With いびきを, means to produce the snoring sound.

guides.explanation_en: 悪くなる combines 悪い (“bad”) in its く-form, 悪く, with なる (“become”). It means that something becomes bad or worse; when it refers to a person's physical condition, it means that the person becomes unwell.

parts.contribution_en: The く-form of 悪い (“bad”), describing the state something changes into.
“Become”; marks a change into the state described by 悪く.

guides.explanation_en: し follows a clause and connects it to another, adding it as one item in a list of facts or reasons. The list often feels open-ended, suggesting that other points may apply too.
もっとも describes a view or claim as reasonable or quite right. もっともだ is a common way to say that something makes sense.
親子 combines 親 (parent) and 子 (child) to refer to them together as a parent-and-child pair. It can describe either the people or their relationship.

parts.contribution_en: parent
child

guides.explanation_en: いつも means “always” or “usually”: it describes something that happens habitually or is generally true. It can suggest every time, though in ordinary use it can also mean regularly without being literally constant.
食う means “to eat.” It is a casual, often blunt-sounding alternative to 食べる, so it is common in informal speech but can sound rough in some settings.
たり marks an action or state as one example in a non-exhaustive list. With する, たりする means to do things such as those listed; repeating たり can give several examples.

parts.contribution_en: Marks an action or state as an example in a non-exhaustive list.
Completes the construction as “do”; together with たり, it gives the sense “do things such as …”.

guides.explanation_en: 仕方 combines 仕, “doing,” with 方, “way or method”: it is a way of doing or handling something. ない says that no such way is available, giving 仕方ない the sense that something cannot be avoided or helped; it often conveys resignation.

parts.contribution_en: doing; the action or matter at hand
way or method
says that the way or method is unavailable

guides.explanation_en: 家の者 means the people of a household, usually its family or other members. の links 家, the home or household, with 者, people, marking their association with it.

parts.contribution_en: home or household
links the household to people associated with it
people

guides.explanation_en: 今でも means “even now” or “still.” 今 names the present time, and でも gives it “even” emphasis, presenting the present as a point up to which something remains true.

parts.contribution_en: the present time; now
adds “even” emphasis to the time expression, highlighting that something remains true up to the present

guides.explanation_en: 十坪 means an area of ten tsubo. 十 gives the quantity, and 坪 names the traditional Japanese unit of area.

parts.contribution_en: ten
the traditional Japanese unit of area, tsubo

guides.explanation_en: 知る means to know something or to come to know it by becoming aware of it or finding it out. It covers both gaining knowledge and the resulting state of knowing.

The counter used for animals.

guides.explanation_en: 兄弟 combines 兄 (older brother) and 弟 (younger brother), framing siblings through those two birth-order positions. As a conventional whole, it means sibling or siblings and can refer to people of any gender; that broader usage belongs to the word, not to 弟 alone.

guides.explanation_en: 与える means to give or provide something to someone. It often describes supplying a person or animal with something they need or can use.
買う means to buy something by paying for it. It is used for ordinary purchases.
一日中 means “all day” or “throughout the whole day.” 一日 names the one-day span, and 中 marks that the time continues across that span.

marks continuation throughout that span

guides.explanation_en: Before a noun, ある means “a certain” or “some”: it points to a person, thing, or time without saying exactly which one. The identity is left unspecified, while the noun itself tells you what kind of thing is meant.
まだ marks a situation as continuing up to the present, or as not having reached an expected point yet. With a negative, it commonly means “not yet.”
ページ means one numbered side of a book or other publication. It is used to refer to or count those sides.

parts.contribution_en: sleep
marks a change whereby someone comes to do the action

guides.explanation_en: だんだん describes a change that happens gradually over time, little by little.
突き出る combines 突く, “thrust or jut,” with 出る, “come out.” It describes something jutting beyond the surface or boundary around it; it is intransitive and does not say that someone is pushing it out.

parts.contribution_en: Carries the sense of thrusting or jutting in the compound.
Contributes the sense of coming out or extending beyond a boundary.

guides.explanation_en: 教師 means a teacher, commonly as a professional or formal role. 教 contributes teaching, and 師 identifies a person in a teaching or instructor role; together they name someone who teaches.

parts.contribution_en: teaching
a person in a teaching or instructor role

guides.explanation_en: 別に treats something apart from others, giving it the sense “separately.” It can also mark something as especially notable; with a negative expression, 別に usually means “not particularly” or “not especially.”

parts.contribution_en: Contributes the idea of being separate or set apart.
Makes 別 adverbial, describing how something is treated or regarded.

guides.explanation_en: 答える means to give an answer or reply to a question or other prompt. The reply may be spoken or written.
二倍 means an amount or number equal to two times a reference amount. 二 contributes “two,” and 倍 contributes “multiple” or “times,” combining to mean “double” or “twice as much or as many.”

parts.contribution_en: two
multiple; times

guides.explanation_en: ワットマン (わっとまん) is the Japanese name for Whatman, a paper brand. It refers to paper made under that brand.
金（かね）means money: funds someone has, spends, or receives. お金 is a common polite form, with お added as a prefix.
こんなに means “this much” or “to this extent,” pointing to an amount or degree as notable in the present context. こんな means “this kind of” or “such”; に turns it into a measure of extent or degree.

parts.contribution_en: Points to something as this kind or sort.
Makes こんな describe an amount or degree.

guides.explanation_en: 気持ち is the inner state or bodily sensation a person has. 気持ちがいい describes something that feels pleasant.

parts.contribution_en: A person's mental or bodily state.
The state or feeling one has; it presents 気 as something experienced by a person.

guides.explanation_en: そんなら is a casual spoken alternative to それなら, meaning “in that case” or “then.” It refers to a situation or point just mentioned and introduces a response or consequence.
鳴らす is the transitive counterpart of 鳴る, meaning to make something sound. With an instrument, it means to play it by producing its sound.
木（き）means a tree, and also wood as a material. The context makes clear whether it refers to the living plant or its wood.

広くはない says that something is not wide or spacious. 広い takes the form 広く before the negation; は gives the negated quality a contrastive emphasis, so the phrase denies that it is wide without necessarily saying that it is cramped.

parts.contribution_en: The connective form of 広い, meaning “wide” or “spacious,” which is the quality being denied.
Marks “being wide” as the contrasted or emphasized quality.
Negates the quality expressed by 広く.

guides.explanation_en: After a plain-form statement, らしい presents its content as an inference from clues or reported information: “apparently” or “it seems.” After a noun, it can also mean “like” that thing or “characteristic of” it, describing a resemblance or quality. These uses share the idea of judging something by how it appears or what it suggests.
空腹 describes the stomach as empty and uses that image for hunger. It is a compact noun, often more formal than お腹がすく.

parts.contribution_en: empty; suggests the stomach lacks food
stomach

guides.explanation_en: 寒い (さむい) describes weather or surroundings with a low temperature, and the cold feeling this causes. 寒さ is the related noun meaning “coldness.”
経つ means for time to pass or elapse. For example, 時間が経つ means “time passes.”
出す describes bringing or sending something outward from where it is. It also means to produce a sound by letting it out.
妙（みょう）describes something as strange or peculiar, with an unusual quality. Before a noun, it takes な, as in 妙な話 (a strange story).
やっと means “at last” or “finally.” It marks something as happening only after waiting, difficulty, or delay.

怖がる means “to be afraid of” or “to show fear of.” The suffix がる makes a verb from the adjective 怖い, describing someone who shows signs of fear; it often refers to another person’s or animal’s visible reaction.

parts.contribution_en: The stem of 怖い, expressing the quality of being frightening and, in this verb, the fear someone shows.
Makes a verb from an adjective stem, describing someone as showing signs of that quality or feeling.

investigation_questions.question: What contribution, if any, does 平 make to modern 不平 meaning dissatisfaction or complaint?

guides.explanation_en: 不平 means dissatisfaction with something a person finds unacceptable, often voiced in complaints or shown in attitude. 不 contributes negation, but that alone does not explain the whole meaning; 平’s role in this modern sense remains unresolved.

parts.contribution_en: Contributes negation, though its role alone does not explain the word’s full meaning.
Its contribution to the modern dissatisfaction sense is unresolved; its listed meanings do not establish one here.

sources.title: 不平（読み）フヘイ | コトバンク
sources.summary_en: The page combines the Digital Daijisen and Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten entries. Digital Daijisen defines modern 不平 as being unable to accept something and feeling dissatisfied; it says the word is often used when frustration over unmet demands appears in a person's words or attitude. Nihon Kokugo Daijiten records distinct senses and earliest examples: uneven or non-flat (1275), a troubled or unsettled heart (1477), discontent (1563), unfair or unequal, and not at peace. The entries attest meanings and examples but do not state a derivation among them.

sources.title: 平 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: The character entry lists 平 contributions including flat or level, impartial or equal, and calm or peaceful, and includes 不平 as a compound under 平. It does not specify which contribution, if any, explains the modern sense of 不平.

claims.text_en: The Japanese dictionary evidence supports 不平 as modern dissatisfaction that may be voiced or shown in attitude. Kanjipedia identifies 不 as a negating element, so negation is a supported contribution of 不. The consulted sources do not establish a specific compositional gloss for 平 in this modern sense.

平 has dictionary-listed contributions including 'level/equal' and 'calm/peaceful'. Although Nihon Kokugo Daijiten records a historical 不平 sense of an unsettled heart, the sources do not establish that 'calm/peaceful' is the active contribution of 平 in the modern complaint or dissatisfaction sense.

Nihon Kokugo Daijiten documents several distinct senses of 不平, including unevenness, an unsettled heart, discontent, unfairness or inequality, and lack of peace. These attestations do not by themselves prove that any one sense or component meaning developed into the modern dissatisfaction sense.

guides.explanation_en: 崩れる means to collapse, crumble, or fall apart. It describes something losing its shape or support and breaking down.
増長 combines 増, “increase,” and 長, “grow,” giving the idea of something growing or increasing. With する, it describes conceit or arrogance growing until someone becomes conceited or arrogant.

Contributes the idea of growing.

investigation_questions.question: Can the historical association between 奥 and wives’ inner quarters be shown to directly explain 奥 in 奥様 and 奥さん?

guides.explanation_en: 奥さん is a conversational honorific for another person’s wife and can also be used as a respectful form of address, like “Mrs.” or “madam.” It is a somewhat more colloquial form of 奥様. Historically, 奥 referred to inner household quarters and could extend to a high-status man’s wife, a possible bridge to the word’s modern meaning.

parts.contribution_en: Historically associated with the inner part of a household and, by extension, a high-status man’s wife; how directly this history shaped 奥さん is not established.
Honorific suffix; in 奥さん, it forms a respectful way to refer to or address someone’s wife.

sources.title: 奥様（読み）オクサマ - コトバンク
sources.summary_en: The page reproduces Digital Daijisen's definitions of 奥様 as an honorific for another person's wife or a female head of household, with historical use for wives of court nobles and daimyo later broadening. The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten entry says 奥さん is a somewhat more colloquial form changed from 奥様 and gives an earliest cited example dated 1761. A separate encyclopedia entry says 奥方 and 奥様 are thought to have arisen because wives' quarters in Momoyama- and Edo-period daimyo residences were toward the rear. That account is explicitly conjectural.

sources.title: 奥（読み）オク - コトバンク
sources.summary_en: The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten records 奥 for an inner part of a house, including a room where family members, wives, and children stayed, and for the restricted inner quarters of high-ranking samurai residences where wives and female attendants lived. It also records a transferred use of 奥 for a high-status person's wife, first cited in an example from 1686.

claims.text_en: The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten analyzes 奥さん as a somewhat more colloquial form changed from 奥様 and dates its earliest cited example to 1761. This supports the word's honorific history, but a first citation does not establish when or how the form originated.

Dictionaries record 奥 both for household inner spaces and, by extension, for a high-status man's wife. This supports an historical association between 奥 and wives' inner quarters, but does not by itself show that modern 奥さん has an independently active spatial meaning.

A Heibonsha encyclopedia account says 奥方 and 奥様 are thought to have arisen because elite wives' quarters were situated toward the rear of residences. It presents this as a likely explanation, not a proven derivation. Since 奥さん is dictionary-analyzed as a form of 奥様, the account offers a plausible historical explanation for its 奥 element, while leaving the direct historical pathway unproven.

guides.explanation_en: それ points back to something already mentioned, and から marks it as the starting point. Together, それから means “after that” or “then,” and can introduce the next item in a sequence.

guides.explanation_en: たくさん means a large quantity or number, and can come before a verb to describe having or doing something in large quantity. 沢山 is a conventional spelling; its characters do not explain the word’s modern meaning.
guides.caveat_en: The original motivation for this spelling has not been established.

sources.title: 沢山（読み）タクサン — コトバンク（デジタル大辞泉・精選版 日本国語大辞典）
sources.summary_en: The entries define たくさん as a large quantity or number and document adverbial use. The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten cites an early example from The Tale of the Heike (13th century). Its note presents the proposed さはやま account, but says examples of さはやま are later and may instead be a kun-reading of たくさん written 沢山. The note describes さは as an old word for many and やま as also expressing numerical abundance; this supports reporting the proposal, not treating it as proven.

sources.title: 沢山／たくさん — 語源由来辞典
sources.summary_en: This etymology reference presents さは (‘many’) plus やま (‘many’) as a proposed source of たくさん, while noting that recorded さはやま examples are later than the Heike example of たくさん. It calls the origin uncertain. Its account is not independent proof of the proposed derivation.

sources.title: たくさん — ウィクショナリー日本語版
sources.summary_en: The entry cites a 1979 Shinmeikai Kokugo Jiten attribution of the origin as unknown and labels 沢山 and 卓散 ateji. It gives the quantity sense ‘many’ and an adverb sense equivalent to ‘in large numbers.’ This is a collaboratively edited reference, not a primary historical source.

sources.title: 沢山 — Wiktionary
sources.summary_en: The entry labels the readings 沢=たく and 山=さん as ateji, says the spelling appears phonetic, and reports the word in The Tale of the Heike. It also gives later usage of さわやま. These are secondary, compiled statements; they do not establish the word’s derivation.

claims.text_en: For the supplied sense, たくさん means that the quantity or number is large. Japanese dictionary entries also document its use as an adverb before a verb, as in 本を沢山持っている.

The consulted references treat 沢山 as an ateji or apparently phonetic spelling for たくさん. The modern quantity sense is therefore not explained by reading 沢 and 山 as ordinary modern components meaning ‘marsh’ and ‘mountain.’ This describes the spelling and current word use; it does not settle how the spelling arose.

One proposed historical explanation combines さは, described in the Nihon Kokugo Daijiten note as an old expression for ‘many,’ with やま, also associated there with numerical abundance, then reads 沢山 with on-readings as たくさん. The same note cautions that recorded さはやま examples are later than the early たくさん example and allows that さはやま may instead be a kun-reading of 沢山. The derivation remains a hypothesis.

The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten lists a たくさん example from The Tale of the Heike, dated to the 13th century, and treats さわやま as a later, Edo-period kun-reading. This chronology challenges a simple claim that the recorded さわやま form gave rise to たくさん, but by itself does not establish the word’s origin.

か marks a question. Within a larger sentence, it closes an embedded question that acts as part of the sentence: for a yes-or-no question it expresses “whether,” while with a question word, that word supplies the information being asked about. At the end of a sentence, か marks a direct question.

sources.title: か(カ)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク
sources.summary_en: The page includes both Digital Daijisen and the Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten. Digital Daijisen describes modern sentence-final か as marking a question, and says the older clause-marking use expanded toward the sentence-final use as the older particle や declined. The Seisenban dictionary documents older clause-internal interrogative and rhetorical uses, gives historical attestations, and describes sentence-final interrogative use as a later grammatical category in its account. These are dictionary descriptions of grammatical history, not evidence for the particle’s ultimate origin.

sources.title: BTS00101 - かどうか/疑問詞…か | みんなの教材サイト
sources.summary_en: The Japan Foundation resource says かどうか forms a nominalized question without an interrogative word, while interrogative word…か forms one that contains an interrogative word. It gives examples with 知る, 聞く, 分かる, 調べる, and other predicates, and says these clauses function as sentence constituents.

claims.text_en: In the described contemporary construction, かどうか marks an embedded yes/no question, while interrogative word…か marks an embedded question containing an interrogative word. The resulting clause functions as a constituent of a larger sentence.

In どこで生まれたか分かりません and 誰がとったか分からない, the interrogative word supplies the requested information and か marks the question clause embedded with 分かる. Translating this use as whether in every instance would be too broad; the supplied English glosses themselves also reflect that distinction.
The supplied quoted question どちらが偉いか ends in interrogative か. The dictionary also gives a contemporary sentence-final question example, 君も行きますか.

The dictionary records older clause-internal interrogative or rhetorical か and describes the expansion of sentence-final use over time. Its classification notes distinguish historical sentence-final cases from the later modern sentence-final particle category; this history does not establish a proven derivation or ultimate etymology.

claims.text_en: 誰（だれ） is an indefinite person pronoun referring to someone whose name or identity is unknown or unclear. The dictionary also records its use in 誰か for an unspecified person and in 誰も with negation for a comprehensive negative meaning.

The older Japanese reading was たれ: the dictionary records it in examples from the Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720). It describes だれ as becoming general in the early-modern period and says the shift is thought to date from its later part; a historical-language paper likewise contrasts older タレ with ダレ and treats ダレ as unavailable in ancient-to-medieval materials. These sources support a change in reading, but do not prove a deeper derivation or component analysis of the Japanese pronoun.

sources.summary_en: The National Diet Library record identifies Yao Yao’s 2022 article in 国語学研究, pages 182–196, and lists subject terms including adverbialization and questioning. The opened record supplies bibliographic metadata only, not the article’s argument or evidence.

claims.text_en: In the interrogative-adverb use, 一体 marks strong questioning and may convey reproach. In the supplied example, it emphasizes the question asking what the addressee is; the dictionaries’ matching sense supports a reusable explanation such as 'what on earth?' or 'what exactly?' rather than separate translations for 一 and 体.

A linguistic analysis likewise treats ittai as an adverb in questions and associates it with an attitude such as impatience or annoyance. That analysis concerns the word’s function, not a semantic contribution from each kanji.

The dictionary describes a usage path within 一体 as a whole: from a generalizing adverbial sense ('generally; in broad outline') to a use that especially strengthens a question or serves in reproach. It records an 1843 example of the questioning use. This supports historical development as relevant context, but does not by itself establish every step or mechanism.

Yamaguchi’s article abstract reports an additional retrospective use, roughly 'in the first place' or 'really,' in literary works from the Meiji, Taisho, and early Showa periods, and says the frequencies of the reported uses change over time. Because only the abstract was available in the opened repository record, its detailed evidence cannot be assessed here.

A cautious modern component-based interpretation is compatible with the dictionary evidence: 本 has a prefix sense for the matter or person currently at issue, and 人 means ‘person.’ This is a semantic inference from separate dictionary entries, not a dictionary-confirmed analysis of 本人 or proof that its meaning is fully compositional.

The separate prefix sense of 本 for something concerning the speaker is illustrated by 本大臣. That sense does not establish 本人 as a first-person pronoun; the dictionary’s central definition identifies the person concerned with the matter.

The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten records additional senses of 本人, including ‘leader’ and ‘instigator,’ and gives a circa 1212–1215 example for the central ‘person directly concerned’ sense. These entries document recorded usage, not the compound’s origin or derivation.

claims.text_en: The dictionary distinguishes older noun uses of おまえ, including a respectful expression for being before a deity or noble person and an indirect respectful reference to a noble person, from its second-person pronoun use. The dictionary labels お as a prefix in its おまえ entries. Separately, it records a noun use of おまえ for the honored space before a deity or noble person, and 前 has an attested spatial sense of the direction one faces. These facts support describing an older honorific spatial association. They do not establish that お and 前 retain independently compositional meanings in the modern second-person pronoun.

The dictionary explicitly says that the historical relationship among the Japanese forms おまえ and おんまえ and Sino-Japanese ごぜん is unclear. The exact pathway from the earlier honorific and spatial uses to the modern second-person pronoun is therefore not established by these sources.

guides.explanation_en: それほど combines それ, “that,” with ほど, “degree or extent,” to mean “that much” or “to that extent.” With a negative expression, it commonly means “not that much” or “not so.”

parts.contribution_en: Points to a degree or amount as “that.”
Marks degree or extent.

guides.explanation_en: 袋（ふくろ）means a bag or sack: a container with an opening for putting things in and taking them out. It can refer to bags of different sizes and materials.

何も combines 何, “what,” with the particle も, which gives the question word broad scope. With a negative predicate, it means that there is nothing in that scope; English may express this as “nothing” or “anything” with a negative.

parts.contribution_en: Names the thing or things in question: “what.”
A particle that gives 何 broad scope, yielding “anything at all” with a negative predicate.

guides.explanation_en: 三つ (みっつ) counts three things using the general native counter つ, when a more specific counter is not used. It can also state that someone is three years old, especially a young child.

parts.contribution_en: The number three.
The general native counter used to count things, and in this form to state an age.

guides.explanation_en: 少し means “a little” or “to a small degree.” With も, the phrase highlights even that small amount; alongside a negative, 少しも means “not even a little” or “not at all.”

parts.contribution_en: “A little” or “to a small degree”; indicates a small amount or degree.
Highlights even the small amount or degree; with a negative, helps form “not even a little.”

guides.explanation_en: 美学 names the study or philosophy of beauty: 美 contributes “beauty,” and 学 marks it as a field of study. It concerns how beauty is understood and what makes things beautiful.

parts.contribution_en: beauty
field of study

guides.explanation_en: 寝床 combines 寝る, “to sleep,” with 床, a floor, platform, or bed to lie on. Together, 寝床 means a bed or other place for sleeping.

parts.contribution_en: Sleeping; from 寝る, “to sleep.”
A floor, platform, or bed to lie on; here, a place for sleeping.

guides.explanation_en: もの is a broad noun for an unspecified thing or matter; context supplies what it refers to. With an adjective such as ひどい, it names the thing or matter as having that quality, so ひどいものだ can mean “that’s awful.”
進む means to move or proceed forward along a route or course. It can also describe something advancing through a process or toward a next stage.
しかも links an added point to what has already been stated, like “moreover” or “besides.” The added point often strengthens the impression or feels noteworthy or unexpected.
だが connects an assertion to a contrasting or qualifying point, meaning “but” or “however.” だ presents the preceding statement in plain form, and が marks the connection as contrastive.

parts.contribution_en: Plain copula that presents the preceding statement as an assertion.
Connects the assertion to what follows with a contrast, giving だが its “but” or “however” meaning.

guides.explanation_en: 日（ひ）means the sun and, by extension, the sunlight it gives. It also means a day, understood as a stretch of time associated with daylight, or simply a particular day.
ふわふわ evokes a soft, light, buoyant quality. With する, it describes feeling that way: light or buoyant, as if floating.

parts.contribution_en: Evokes a soft, light, buoyant quality.
Turns that quality into a state or feeling.

guides.explanation_en: 困る means to be in difficulty or at a loss about how to manage a situation. In the pattern 食べ物に困る, it means to have difficulty getting food, and so to lack enough food.
給料 means wages or salary, and 日 means day. Together, 給料日 is the day wages or salary are paid: payday.

parts.contribution_en: wages or salary
day; marks when wages or salary are paid

guides.explanation_en: 気づく means to notice something or become aware of it; when what comes to attention is its meaning or significance, it can mean to realize. 気 contributes the idea of awareness or attention, while 付く, written づく here, pictures that awareness as coming to rest on something.

parts.contribution_en: A person's awareness or attention.
The verb 付く, written in kana here, contributes the idea of coming to rest or attach; with 気, it conveys awareness settling on something.

guides.explanation_en: 投げる means to throw something, sending it through the air with a forceful movement. The object may be aimed at a target or thrown away.
者（もの） means a person or individual. It often refers to someone identified by a description, with the sense “the person who …” or “one who …”.

investigation_questions.question: What, if any, distinct contribution does 懸命 make to the modern meaning of 一生懸命?

guides.explanation_en: 一生懸命 means acting with great effort and earnest commitment, sometimes with a desperate or life-risking force. It developed from 一所懸命, an older expression for defending a livelihood-bearing holding at risk of life that later came to describe desperate effort; the modern form became familiar as the place-related association faded.
guides.caveat_en: The history supports a link to the older expression, but not a reliable literal reading of 一生 as “one’s whole life.”

parts.contribution_en: The spelling developed from 一所 in the older form, where it referred to one place or holding; 一生 does not reliably contribute “one’s whole life” to the modern meaning.
The supplied evidence does not establish a separate modern contribution for this part; the whole expression conveys earnest effort, sometimes with desperate or life-risking force.

sources.title: 一生懸命（読み）イッショウケンメイ - コトバンク（精選版 日本国語大辞典・デジタル大辞泉・四字熟語を知る辞典）
sources.summary_en: The entries define 一生懸命 as facing something with life-risking seriousness, making a concentrated effort, or acting earnestly. They say it changed from 一所懸命 and give a 1734 Jōruri example as the earliest cited example for the earnest-effort sense. The 日本国語大辞典 word-history note proposes that changes in landholding concepts and a shift in the associations of 一生—from lifelong duration toward something momentous, as in 一生の—contributed to the change. The 四字熟語を知る辞典 separately points to phonetic similarity between 一所 and 一生 as a reason the forms were mixed.

sources.title: 一所懸命（読み）イッショケンメイ - コトバンク（精選版 日本国語大辞典・デジタル大辞泉）
sources.summary_en: The dictionary records 一所懸命 for a medieval landholding treated as a livelihood and defended at risk of life, with a cited example from 古事談 (1212–15). It records a figurative urgent or life-risking sense by 智恵鑑 (1660). Its word-history note says that the place-related sense weakened, leaving the desperate-effort sense, and that the expression is thought to have changed form to 一生懸命 as the place/estate association faded.

sources.title: 第197回「一“所”懸命」 - 日本語、どうでしょう？（ジャパンナレッジ）
sources.summary_en: Explains 一所 as one place and describes a shift from protecting a landholding to the general meanings ‘life-risking’ and ‘desperate,’ followed by a change to the similar-sounding 一生. The author suggests that the more familiar 一生 and a changed Edo-period association of 一生 may have helped the change; these are presented as explanations, not direct demonstrations. The article says both spellings are acceptable and that 一生懸命 is now more common.

sources.title: 一生懸命 - スピーチに役立つ四字熟語辞典（イミダス）
sources.summary_en: Defines the word as putting effort into something with life-risking seriousness and says it changed from 一所懸命. It traces the older expression to a medieval warrior’s landholding that had to be protected at risk of life.

sources.title: イッショウケンメイ | 言葉 | 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: Defines 一生懸命 as facing something with life-risking seriousness or engaging with it earnestly, and notes briefly that it developed from 一所懸命.

sources.title: 「一所懸命」から「一生懸命」へ - 国立国語研究所 日本語研究・日本語教育文献データベース
sources.summary_en: Catalog record for Shinichi Narumi’s 2007 article in 国語学研究 46, pages 130–118. Its keywords include figurative transfer, 一生, and lengthening. The catalog record confirms the article’s subject and scope but does not give its argument or evidence.

claims.text_en: For present-day use, explain 一生懸命 as acting with great effort and earnest commitment; depending on context, it can also carry a desperate or life-risking sense. The dictionaries support these meanings, including examples of working and searching 一生懸命. Treat it as an established whole-word meaning.

The older form 一所懸命 referred to a medieval holding or estate that was a basis of livelihood and was defended at risk of life. It later had a figurative sense of urgent, desperate, or life-risking action. The dictionary’s cited examples date the landholding sense to 1212–15 and the figurative sense to 1660; these are cited attestations, not proof of the expression’s first use.

Dictionaries identify 一生懸命 as a changed form of 一所懸命 and cite an example of the modern form from 1734. Their proposed account connects the form change with the fading of the place/estate association and the generalized desperate-effort sense. The precise steps and causes are proposed word-history explanations, not established by the citation dates alone.

Do not teach 一生 as reliably contributing the compositional meaning ‘one’s whole life’ in present-day 一生懸命. The sources define the compound as a whole. One dictionary proposes that changed associations of 一生, including its use for something momentous or occurring once in a lifetime, may have helped motivate the form; other explanations emphasize sound similarity and familiarity. These accounts do not establish ‘one’s whole life’ as the modern compound’s literal meaning.

A narrowly supported component note can say that 一所 in the older form referred to one place or holding, and that the familiar 一生懸命 developed from that older expression as its place-related sense weakened. Do not split the modern compound into independent literal contributions to gloss its current meaning.

gaps: The full text of Narumi’s 2007 scholarly article was not available in the opened catalog record, so its detailed evidence and account of lengthening and the transition to 一生懸命 could not be checked.

The opened dictionary and JapanKnowledge accounts agree on a development from 一所懸命 but differ in the proposed factors behind the change: fading landholding associations, phonetic similarity, and shifts in the associations or familiarity of 一生. Their relative roles and exact chronology remain unsettled by the sources opened.

The Education Publishing page could not be read through the web access used here, so its claim that the ‘whole life’ interpretation is folk etymology was not independently verified and is not relied on.

research_questions: 一生懸命 is commonly connected historically to 一所懸命. What evidence establishes that development, and how did the spelling and meaning change?

In present-day Japanese, does 一生 make a reliable semantic contribution to 一生懸命, or is treating it as “one’s whole life” a later reinterpretation? What should the reusable entry say about the compound’s parts?

guides.explanation_en: ずいぶん indicates a substantial degree or amount, often with a sense that it is more than one might expect. It commonly modifies adjectives and verbs, and can also describe a noun in the form ずいぶんな + noun.
めったにない means that something hardly ever happens or is hardly ever the case. めったに marks very low frequency and normally combines with a negative predicate such as ない.

parts.contribution_en: Marks very low frequency and normally occurs with a negative predicate.
Negates the predicate, completing the expression for something that hardly ever happens or is the case.

guides.explanation_en: 繰り返す means to do or say something again. 繰り evokes working through something in sequence, and 返す adds the idea of returning to it: together they frame repetition as coming back to an action or sequence and doing it again.

parts.contribution_en: The stem of 繰る, evoking turning or working through something in sequence.
To return; here, it suggests coming back to the action or sequence.

guides.explanation_en: また means “again”: it says that an action or event happens one more time. It commonly appears before the action it describes.
捨てる is a simple Japanese verb meaning to throw something away or give it up, ending one’s keeping or commitment to it. With a person or responsibility, it can mean to abandon them.
いじめる means to bully or mistreat someone by treating them harshly or causing distress. It can describe repeated bullying or a particular act of mistreatment.
男 means “man” or “male person.” It is a noun for identifying a person as male and also appears in compounds and expressions about men.

そこ means “that place” or “there,” referring to a place associated with the listener or already established in the conversation. Particles such as へ can show movement toward it, while は can mark it as the topic.
それ points to something associated with the listener or already identified in the conversation or situation. It can mean “that” or “it,” depending on what it refers to.

便所 combines 便, referring here to bodily waste or relieving oneself, with 所, “place.” Together they name a place for using the toilet. 便所 is a direct, somewhat old-fashioned term; トイレ is more usual in everyday speech.

parts.contribution_en: Bodily waste or the act of relieving oneself; here, the toilet function.
Place; identifies where that function takes place.

guides.explanation_en: こと follows a clause or verb phrase and lets it function as a noun phrase: 走ること means “running” or “the act of running.” The nominalized content can be referred to as a fact, event, or matter.
With 名前 as its object, つける means to give or assign a name to someone or something. The name is treated as something added to its bearer; the person or thing receiving the name can be marked with に.

持つ (もつ) means to hold or carry something. It also means to have or possess something, extending the idea of keeping it in one’s hands or under one’s control. With movement or a destination, it can mean to take something along.
乗せる means to place something on a surface or support. With a person and a vehicle or other conveyance, it means to put them aboard and let them ride.
送る means to send or dispatch something toward a destination. The destination is commonly marked with へ or に.

After a plain verb, よう presents the state or pattern in which that action happens, に marks it as the state reached, and なる means “become.” Together, Vようになる means that someone or something comes to do V or that V begins to happen as a new habit or state.

parts.contribution_en: Presents the state or pattern in which the preceding action happens.
Marks that state as the result reached.
Means “become” and describes a change into that state.

guides.explanation_en: 女の人 means “woman” or “adult female person.” 女 identifies the person as female, and の links it to 人 (“person”), so the phrase names a person by gender.

parts.contribution_en: Identifies the person as female.
Links 女 to 人 in a noun-modifying relation.
Means “person”; with 女の, it refers to a woman.

guides.explanation_en: 震える means to tremble or shiver: to shake with small, often involuntary movements, as from cold, fear, or strong emotion.
こんな points to something as being of this kind or having this sort of quality. It modifies a noun directly: こんな本 means “this kind of book.”
たたく means to strike or hit something with a hand or an object. It can describe one blow or repeated blows, depending on the action.
失う means to lose something or cease to have it. It can refer to losing possessions or opportunities, or to losing qualities such as health or trust.
竹垣 means a fence made of bamboo. 竹 contributes “bamboo,” and 垣 contributes “fence,” so together they name a bamboo fence.

parts.contribution_en: bamboo
fence

guides.explanation_en: The particle で marks the setting or basis for an action or statement: where or when something happens, what means or cause is involved, or the role or group within which something applies. The phrase before で supplies that setting or basis. In でも, も adds the sense of “even”; in 話では, で marks the report as the basis for what follows, while は presents it as the topic or frame.
つるつる describes a surface that is very smooth and often slick. For skin or a head, it can also mean smooth and hairless.
すべきだ means “should” or “ought to do.” The す from する names the action, べき marks it as advisable or required, and だ states that judgment directly.

parts.contribution_en: Names the action with する (“do”), in the form used before べき.
Marks the action as advisable or required.
States the judgment directly.

guides.explanation_en: 三ページ means three pages. 三 gives the number, and ページ names the unit being counted; this pattern works with other numbers too.

parts.contribution_en: Three.
Page; the unit being counted.

guides.explanation_en: 主人（しゅじん）means the master or head of a household: the person who holds the principal role in it.

parts.contribution_en: The principal or person in charge.
A person; here, the person with the principal role in the household.

guides.explanation_en: だけに marks a reason as especially relevant: because something is true, a related result follows all the more. It can also highlight that the result is fitting or striking in light of that reason.
手のひら is the inner surface of the hand, from the wrist to the bases of the fingers. 手 means “hand,” の links it to ひら, “flat surface” or “side,” giving the sense of the hand’s flat inner surface.

parts.contribution_en: hand
links “hand” to the surface associated with it
flat surface or side; here, the inner surface of the hand

guides.explanation_en: こと lets the preceding verb phrase be treated as an action, and も marks that action as an addition (“also”) or, especially under negation, as an emphatic “even.” する means to carry out the action, so Vこともする means to do V too or even do V; Vこともしない means not even do V.

parts.contribution_en: Turns the preceding verb phrase into an action that can be treated as something to do.
Marks the action as an addition (“also”); under negation, it can emphasize “even.”
Means “do” or “carry out” and supplies the main verb.

guides.explanation_en: 子猫 combines 子, which marks a young animal here, with 猫, “cat.” The compound means a young cat, or kitten.

parts.contribution_en: marks the animal as young
cat

guides.explanation_en: そして connects what follows to what came before. Depending on the relationship, it adds a point (“and”) or moves the sequence forward (“and then”).

のに follows a clause and marks a contrast: what follows is unexpected given what came before. It means “although,” “even though,” or “despite the fact that,” and can convey disappointment or complaint.
乗る means to get onto something and be carried or supported by it, or to travel while on it. It is used with vehicles, surfaces, and people; the natural English wording depends on what one gets onto.
一つ (ひとつ) counts one item or one instance. The native counting ending つ lets it count things without naming a more specific counter.

parts.contribution_en: Supplies the count of one, read ひと in this form.
A native counting ending used here to count items or instances.

guides.explanation_en: 玉（たま）means a jewel or a bead: a valued stone polished for its beauty, or a small piece used as an ornament, often strung with others. The word covers both precious stones and decorative beads.
話す means to speak or talk, and also to tell something by expressing it in words. It can refer either to speaking generally or to communicating particular content.

investigation_questions.question: Does 間 make a distinct, reliable contribution to the modern にんげん meaning?

guides.explanation_en: 人間 means a human being or person, whether people generally or one individual. Its modern meaning is not reliably explained by adding up the characters; historically, the word referred to the human realm before it came to refer to a being living in that realm.

sources.title: 人間(ニンゲン)とは？ 意味や使い方 — コトバンク
sources.summary_en: Digital Daijisen lists にんげん senses including human beings, a particular person, character/personality, and the human world. The Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten records a Buddhist human-realm sense with a 984 example and a human/person sense with an example from a work dated around 1120; these are earliest cited examples in that dictionary, not proof of the word’s origin. The Nipponica encyclopedia says the word was originally a Buddhist term used like 世間 and later came to be used in everyday speech for a being who lives in the human realm.

sources.title: Watsuji Tetsurō’s Ethics of Milieu — Pauline Couteau
sources.summary_en: In its discussion of Watsuji Tetsurō, the chapter renders ningen 人間 as a person in an interstice and explains the spatial, individual, and communal dimensions of human existence in that philosophical account. This supports an interpretation associated with Watsuji, not a demonstrated historical derivation or a general rule for modern Japanese word meaning.

sources.title: 間 — ウィクショナリー日本語版
sources.summary_en: The Japanese entry lists 間 meanings including physical, temporal, and abstract intervals, as well as connection or relations between people. Its examples and definitions establish possibilities for 間 in Japanese but do not establish its contribution to 人間（にんげん）.

claims.text_en: Modern Japanese dictionaries give 人間（にんげん） the sense ‘human being; person.’ The dictionary record also documents an older Buddhist human-realm sense. Its dated citations show a cited Buddhist example from 984 and a human/person example from a work dated around 1120; they do not by themselves establish the word’s derivation or the exact path of semantic change.

間 has Japanese senses such as interval, between, and relation between people. This evidence does not establish that 間 reliably contributes ‘between people’ or ‘social relation’ to the modern にんげん sense ‘human being/person.’ The dictionary separately records 人間（じんかん） with a world/society sense, which should not be conflated with the supplied にんげん headword.

Pauline Couteau’s discussion of Watsuji Tetsurō presents a philosophical reading of ningen as a person in an interstice and relates human existence to both individual and communal dimensions. This attests a philosophical interpretation; it does not prove the compound’s historical derivation or show that ordinary modern usage compositionally carries that interpretation.

The Nipponica encyclopedia describes 人間 as originally a Buddhist term used with a meaning like 世間 and says it later came to be used in everyday speech for a being living in the human realm. This is a dictionary/encyclopedia account of semantic history, not evidence that 間 contributes a dependable ‘between people’ meaning in current 人間（にんげん）.

guides.explanation_en: いる means “to exist” or “to be present” when speaking of living things.

After a noun or な-adjective, ではない forms its plain negative: “is not” or “are not.” で connects the description to the copula, は marks it as the point being denied and can add contrast, and ない makes the predicate negative.

parts.contribution_en: Connects a noun or な-adjective to the copula.
Marks the description as the point being denied and can add contrast.
Makes the predicate negative.

guides.explanation_en: 不人望 means being unpopular or lacking other people’s favor and regard. 不 marks the absence of 人望, the esteem or regard a person receives from others.

parts.contribution_en: Marks the absence of the following 人望.
Esteem or regard a person receives from others.

guides.explanation_en: 続く（つづく）means to continue or last over time. It describes an activity, state, or event that carries on.
耐える means to keep bearing something difficult or unpleasant without succumbing to it. The hardship is commonly marked with に, as in 痛みに耐える (endure pain).
はずだ presents something as expected or logically likely based on what is known; だ states that expectation plainly. It follows a plain-form verb or い-adjective, a な-adjective with な, or a noun with の.

parts.contribution_en: Frames the following proposition as an expected or logically likely outcome.
States that expectation plainly.

investigation_questions.question: Did やかん arise as a compound, or was 薬缶 adopted later as its conventional spelling?

guides.explanation_en: やかん is a kettle used to heat water. Its name is conventionally explained by its former use for boiling medicine: 薬 points to medicine, and 缶 here represents カン/罐, the vessel. The spelling fits this explanation but does not establish how the word arose.

parts.contribution_en: Medicine, linked to the vessel's conventional name explanation.
The vessel element, written with 缶 for カン/罐.

sources.title: 薬罐（読み）やっかん — 精選版 日本国語大辞典・改訂新版 世界大百科事典
sources.summary_en: The National Language Dictionary entry defines やかん as a kettle-like water-heating vessel, explains the name by its former use for boiling medicine, and gives a cited example from 鎌倉殿中以下年中行事 dated circa 1454. The encyclopedia says the graph 薬罐 first appears in 下学集 (1444), calls やかん the Sino-Japanese reading of 薬罐, and reports a shift to heating water and tea by the Edo period. These are reference-work reports; the primary texts were not examined here.

sources.title: 薬缶（読み）ヤカン — デジタル大辞泉・食器・調理器具がわかる辞典
sources.summary_en: The entries define やかん as a water-heating utensil and explain the name by its earlier use for decocting medicine. They do not establish how the word or spelling originated.

sources.title: ヤカン — 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: Defines 薬缶 as a water-heating vessel and attributes the name to its use for decocting medicine. This supports the conventional medicine-related explanation, not a proven account of the compound's formation.

sources.title: 缶 — 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: Distinguishes the Japanese-use 缶 read カン, used for 罐 and found in 薬缶, from 缶 read フ meaning a pottery vessel. Its character note supports the container association of the カン/罐 form, while also noting that modern 缶 is a Japanese conventional form.

sources.title: 缶（読み）カン — デジタル大辞泉・精選版 日本国語大辞典・普及版 字通
sources.summary_en: The Digital Daijisen character entry lists 湯わかし器 as a sense of カン and 薬缶 as an example; it says 罐 originally referred to a well-bucket and is now represented by 缶. The page also distinguishes these uses from 缶 read フ, a pottery vessel. It does not by itself establish the historical derivation of やかん.

sources.title: くすり — 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: Defines くすり as a medicine used to treat or prevent illness or injury, among other senses. This supports the modern medicine contribution of 薬 as a character; it does not prove when or why 薬 was assigned in this compound.

claims.text_en: Modern やかん (薬缶/薬罐) means a vessel for heating water, commonly translated “kettle.” The cited Japanese references explain the name by the vessel's former use for decocting or boiling medicine.

The encyclopedia reports that やかん became mainly a water- and tea-heating vessel by the Edo period after a separate pot came to be used for boiling medicine. This is a reported historical account, not a directly verified primary-text chronology here.

Reference works report 薬罐 in 下学集 (1444) and cite a kettle-related example from 鎌倉殿中以下年中行事 (circa 1454). These establish reported medieval written attestations, but the underlying texts were not opened for direct verification.

The written characters are consistent with 薬 “medicine” plus the カン/罐 container element: Japanese references connect the vessel's name with its medicinal use, and character references identify 缶 as a conventional Japanese form used for 罐, with container-related カン uses. This supports a modern component interpretation, but does not prove the compound was coined compositionally or establish whether the reading or spelling arose through borrowing or another convention.

claims.text_en: Japanese dictionaries attest 一部 as a counter or noun for one complete book, or a complete set of printed material, alongside its separate sense ‘a part of a whole.’ This book sense is the one identified in dictionary explanations of the older 一部始終 expression.

Dictionaries describe the expression’s earlier sense as the beginning-to-end of a book and its event sense as the course of events from beginning to end. claims.text_en: For the requested sense, dictionaries describe noun-attached 次第 as expressing dependence on a person's intention or on a matter's circumstances. In the supplied example, 自分の気分しだい means that what the speaker does depends on his mood; this application follows the dictionary definition and the supplied context.

A limited modern semantic association is supportable: 次第 also has noun senses such as order, course, and circumstances, while 次 and 第 each have Japanese dictionary associations with order or sequence. A course or circumstances can serve as the factor on which an outcome depends, but the sources opened do not establish this as the historical path by which the suffix sense developed.

The opened Japanese character entries associate 次 and 第 with order or sequence, but they do not show that either character independently contributes a separable meaning to the modern suffix sense ‘depending on.’ In particular, the character entry for 第 cannot establish its role in that use of the whole word.

A NINJAL catalog record confirms that a scholarly study specifically addresses the suffix use's formation and development, but its bibliographic record alone does not support claims about the study's conclusions. A historical derivation from the components or from the noun senses therefore remains unverified here.

claims.text_en: The consulted dictionaries and JAANUS give 台盤所 as the conventional proposed source of 台所, but phrase the historical connection as an abbreviation or a believed/thought origin. The dictionary dates the shortening to medieval times or later; the materials consulted do not establish a proven derivation.

At the level of 台盤所, 台盤 denotes a legged food-serving stand or low table, and 所 denotes the place where it is set. This supports a compound-level explanation of 台盤所; it does not establish 台 alone as meaning ‘kitchen’ or as independently naming a kitchen space.

The entries distinguish early contexts: 台盤所 is cited from 宇津保物語 (c. 970–999) and described as a palace room for female attendants and food service; 台所 is cited for a cooking and food-service room in 吾妻鏡 (1203). These attestations show the terms in different contexts but do not by themselves demonstrate that one developed from the other.

investigation_questions.question: Is there reliable evidence that 交 contributes a specific part of the Japanese word’s turn-taking sense?
Is there reliable evidence that 番 contributes a specific part of the Japanese word’s turn-taking sense?

guides.explanation_en: 交番 also means “taking turns.” Its police-box sense is shortened from 交番所 and is commonly explained as referring to officers taking turns on watch, though that naming link is conjectural.

sources.title: 交番（読み）コウバン | コトバンク
sources.summary_en: The 精選版 日本国語大辞典 lists a general sense of taking turns doing something and a police-post sense abbreviated from 交番所. It cites 江戸繁昌記 (1832–36) for the general sense and 樋口一葉’s たけくらべ (1895–96) for the police-post sense. These dictionary entries give definitions and cited attestations, not direct evidence for why 交番所 was named.

sources.title: （1）　交番・駐在所の歴史
sources.summary_en: The National Police Agency recounts that in 1874 patrol officers were assigned to designated 交番所 locations. The locations initially had no buildings; officers went there from 屯所 in rotation and stood watch. The account supports the associated work practice but does not state that this is why the location was named.

sources.title: 交番まめ知識 | 警視庁
sources.summary_en: The Tokyo Metropolitan Police says officers in 1874 went from police stations to designated places and took turns standing watch. It suggests that 交番所 was named for being a place where officers took turns keeping watch, wording the explanation as a conjecture (と思われます).

sources.title: 第129回国会　参議院　地方行政委員会　第6号　平成6年6月16日 | テキスト表示 | 国会会議録検索システム シンプル表示
sources.summary_en: In a 1994 committee exchange about the word’s origin, a government official says it is said that 交番所 was used with the sense of a place where officers took turns standing watch, and that 交番 became a familiar shortened form. The qualified wording reports an attributed explanation; it does not cite a Meiji-era naming record.

sources.title: 夜寒十句 | 正岡子規
sources.summary_en: In this literary text, a narrator sees one officer leave a 交番所 as another enters, apparently at a shift change; the accompanying verse uses 交番 and 交代 together. This is an attestation of the association between the post and turn-taking, not evidence of the word’s original naming.

claims.text_en: The 精選版 日本国語大辞典 gives 交番 a general sense of taking turns doing something and defines its police-post sense as an abbreviation of 交番所.

The National Police Agency’s history says that in 1874 officers went in rotation from 屯所 to designated 交番所 locations, where they stood watch. This documents the practice associated with the proposed name explanation, but does not establish that practice as the proven reason for the name.
The Tokyo Metropolitan Police presents “a place where officers take turns standing watch” as a presumed explanation for the name 交番所, explicitly marking it as conjectural.
In a 1994 Diet committee exchange, a government official also reports the turn-taking explanation as something said about the name’s origin, rather than citing direct historical proof.

Masaoka Shiki’s literary text depicts officers changing places at a 交番所 and pairs 交番 with 交代 in a verse. This shows a historical association with turn-taking, but does not prove the original naming rationale.

The dictionary cites 江戸繁昌記 (1832–36) for the general turn-taking sense and たけくらべ (1895–96) for the police-post use. These are the dictionary’s cited first examples, not direct documentation of why 交番所 was named.

investigation_questions.question: Is there evidence for a conventional modern Japanese analysis specifying how 権 and 利 contribute to 権利?

guides.explanation_en: 権利 means a right: a qualification or capacity to act freely or make a claim, including the legal capacity to claim and enjoy a benefit. 権 contributes the association with that qualifying capacity; 利 evokes usefulness or benefit, fitting what may be claimed or enjoyed. One account of the term’s adoption says 利 was added in a translation context where 権 could suggest officials’ authority, helping express what ordinary people were due.
guides.caveat_en: 利 is associated with benefit, but does not itself mean “entitlement” here. The sources do not establish a fixed modern division of the compound’s meaning.

parts.contribution_en: Associated with a qualification or capacity to act or make a claim; it also has a distinct sense of authority.
Associated with usefulness, advantage, or gain, fitting a benefit that may be claimed or enjoyed; its precise contribution in 権利 is not established.

sources.title: 権利(ケンリ)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク
sources.summary_en: Digital Daijisen gives a general sense of 権利 as the qualification or capacity to act freely or make demands, and a legal sense as the capacity to claim and enjoy a benefit. The entry also records a separate sense, “power and benefit.” The Kokusho Daijiten section cites the supplied Natsume Sōseki sentence as an example of the general qualification sense and records an older legal sense as a translation of English right.

sources.summary_en: Lists 権 with meanings including power, a right or qualification, and a weighing weight. This supports the existence of a Japanese character sense related to rights, while the character-history note concerns the character’s development and does not establish the formation of 権利.

sources.title: 利 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: Lists 利 with meanings including usefulness, advantage, and profit or gain, and includes 権利 among compounds. It does not say that 利 by itself means entitlement in 権利.

sources.title: 権(ケン)とは？ 意味や使い方 - コトバンク
sources.summary_en: Digital Daijisen lists 権 as both power to control others and a qualification to act or make claims. Kokusho Daijiten also records senses related to rights, including a qualification to act and a right attached to an office.

sources.title: 受容期における人格概念の内実としての権利・義務概念――その関係依存的解釈と関係規定的解釈：西周を例として
sources.summary_en: Hiroshi Goto’s 2023 scholarly article discusses the modern Japanese adoption of 権利 as a translation for right. It reports that Nishi and Tsuda consulted William Martin’s Chinese translation of Wheaton’s Elements of International Law. It describes Martin’s account that 利 was added because 権 could refer either to officials’ authority or to what ordinary people were due, while noting that the intended nuance of 権利 admits more than one interpretation. This historical discussion does not prove a fixed, transparent modern Japanese component-by-component derivation.

claims.text_en: In modern Japanese, 権利 can mean a qualification or capacity to act freely or make a demand. In legal usage it can mean the capacity to claim and enjoy a benefit. The cited literary example uses the general qualification sense: the first finder has the right to eat the food.

権 has an attested Japanese sense meaning a qualification or capacity to act or make a claim, alongside the distinct sense of power or authority. Thus “power” alone does not cover its relevant association in 権利.

利 is associated in Japanese character references with usefulness, advantage, and profit or gain. These associations are compatible with the benefit that may be claimed or enjoyed under a right, but the references do not establish that 利 independently means “entitlement” in 権利.

A scholarly account of the term’s modern Japanese adoption reports that Martin’s translation added 利 to 権 in a context where 権 alone could suggest officials’ authority, and describes 利 as helping express what ordinary people were due. The same account presents more than one interpretation of the choice, so it does not establish a single proven compositional derivation for modern Japanese 権利.

The dictionary’s older gloss “power and benefit,” its general modern sense, and its legal sense identified as a translation of English right are distinct evidence. The older gloss by itself does not prove that modern 権利 was formed by simply combining the standalone meanings “power” and “benefit.”

guides.explanation_en: 読む（よむ）means to read written text and understand its words. It is used for things such as books, pages, and messages.

After words or a clause, と marks quoted speech, thought, or intended content. After a verb or clause, it can link an event to a natural, predictable, or repeated result, or mark when something happens; with a noun, it marks a companion or joins items in a list. It can also follow a sound or manner expression, or mark a comparison; before 時, it marks the time at which something happens.

parts.contribution_en: A particle whose function depends on what it attaches to: it marks quoted content, event-result or time relations, accompaniment, lists, sounds or manners, and comparisons.

guides.explanation_en: 外（そと）means the outside: the area beyond a boundary, especially the exterior of an enclosed space. It can refer to that area as a place or direction, as in 外へ出る (go outside).

見つめる means to gaze steadily at or stare at something without looking away. One linguistic analysis treats it as 見る plus 詰める: 詰める adds the idea of carrying out the looking to a limit, giving a sustained, fixed gaze; its precise force can depend on what is being looked at.

parts.contribution_en: The continuative form of 見る, “to look,” as the first verb in the compound analysis.
This kana spelling corresponds to 詰める in the compound analysis, where it contributes carrying out the looking to a limit. The spelling 見つめる is also used for the same word as 見詰める.

sources.title: 見詰める（読み）ミツメル — コトバンク（デジタル大辞泉・精選版 日本国語大辞典）
sources.summary_en: Digital Daijisen defines the word as looking steadily at something without taking one’s eyes off it. The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten gives a similar definition and cites an example from Uji Shūi Monogatari, dated around 1221. This is evidence for the whole word’s attestation, not its derivation.

sources.title: みつめる — IPAL『動詞・形容詞の用法』
sources.summary_en: NINJAL lists 見（み）詰（つ）める and 見（み）つめる as spellings of one entry. It defines the word as looking steadily at an object or place without looking away, lists 見る as a superordinate term, and classifies the action as durative. It does not provide a component analysis.

sources.title: 日本語の語彙的複合動詞「V1＋詰める」の意味形成とその認知的メカニズム — 蘇暁笛
sources.summary_en: This scholarly paper includes 見詰める among lexical V1＋詰める compounds. It proposes the construction’s core meaning as performing V1 up to a limit. For looking at a computer screen, it analyzes 見詰める as looking for a long time or continuously, with a temporal limit. For looking at oneself, it gives a different analysis involving a physical limit. This is a proposed analysis of compound meaning, not proof of historical origin.

sources.title: 複合動詞レキシコン｜このサイトについて — 国立国語研究所
sources.summary_en: NINJAL describes the lexicon as covering lexical compounds formed from a verb continuative form plus a verb, and explains that its displayed structural analyses reflect the compiler’s linguistic analysis and are not established doctrine. This supports cautious attribution of compound analyses, but does not specifically analyze 見つめる.

claims.text_en: A supported reusable gloss is “to gaze steadily at; to stare at”: the dictionaries describe looking continuously at an object without taking one’s eyes off it.

A scholarly analysis treats 見詰める as V1＋詰める and proposes that 詰める contributes the idea of carrying out V1 up to a limit. In the paper’s screen example, this means looking for a long time or continuously, with a temporal limit. The contribution varies with the object, so it should not be reduced to persistence in every context. Attribute this as the paper’s analysis, not a settled or historical derivation.

IPAL lists 見つめる and 見詰める as spellings of the same word; the scholarly paper analyzes 見詰める as V1＋詰める. These sources support retaining 見つめる as one lexical entry and, if the data model represents morphology, linking its components as the verb 見る (in its continuative form 見) plus 詰める. They do not support treating the kana string つめる in the mixed spelling as an independent lexical item. This representation recommendation is an inference from the sources, not a rule about a particular database schema.
The Nihon Kokugo Daijiten cites an example of the whole word from Uji Shūi Monogatari, dated around 1221. That attestation does not by itself establish when or how the compound arose.

As a standalone conjunction, ところが introduces something contrary to what the preceding situation led you to expect. A modern functional analysis treats ところ as evoking that situation and contrastive が as marking the unexpected turn. This use differs from clause-linking ところが, which has a different grammatical structure.

parts.contribution_en: Evokes the situation or circumstances being discussed.
Marks contrast with those circumstances.

sources.title: ところが（読み）トコロガ - コトバンク・デジタル大辞泉
sources.summary_en: Separately describes the standalone conjunction as introducing content contrary to what the preceding matter leads one to expect, and the clause-linking particle as formal noun ところ plus case particle が attached to the past auxiliary た. It lists discovery/result and counterfactual-concessive uses for the clause-linking form, notes that the latter use is usually expressed by ところで in modern Japanese, and dates ところが to the late Edo period onward. The date does not establish a derivational history.

sources.title: ‘ところ’の用法について - 正宗美根子, 北陸大学紀要 25 (2001)
sources.summary_en: The paper analyzes ところが synchronically. For clause-linking examples it says が contributes contrast and makes the unexpected relation stronger than ところ alone. For the standalone conjunction it analyzes ところ as followed by contrastive が, connecting a statement contrary to prior expectation. This is a functional analysis, not evidence establishing the historical development of the conjunction.

sources.title: 日本語教育通信 文法を楽しく「ところ」（２） - 国際交流基金
sources.summary_en: Distinguishes clause-internal ところが from the independent conjunction ところが. It explains the conjunction as marking an actual event or situation contrary to expectation, and notes that it is unsuitable for simple opposition or comparison without that unexpectedness.

claims.text_en: As a standalone conjunction, ところが introduces content contrary to what the preceding statement leads one to expect. This matches the supplied translation “however; but”; the particular expectation in the supplied sentence depends on its preceding context.

A modern functional analysis treats the conjunction as ところ plus contrastive が: ところ evokes the situation or preceding circumstance, while が marks contrast, yielding a link to an unexpected development. This is an analysis of present function, not proof of the word’s historical derivation.

The conjunction should be distinguished from clause-linking ところが. The dictionary analyzes the latter as formal noun ところ plus case particle が after past た, with uses including a discovery or result and a counterfactual concession; it notes that modern Japanese usually uses ところで for the concessive use.

claims.text_en: For a reusable modern explanation, 退屈 can describe having nothing to do, feeling bored or fed up, or finding something tedious. Dictionaries also record senses involving weariness, discouragement, and shrinking back before difficulty. In the supplied sentence, 退屈で is best understood in context as “because [I am] bored.”

A cautious modern component gloss is: 退 suggests retreating or withdrawing; 屈 can suggest bending, yielding, or losing resolve. This matches the traditional explanation of the Buddhist sense: when practice is difficult, one's resolve to pursue the path retreats and yields. The match makes a useful mnemonic, but does not show that each character transparently supplies part of every modern sense.

The Buddhist sense is documented in the dictionary with an attestation in 往生要集 dated 984–985. Otani University presents everyday boredom or aversion as a later extension of that sense; Hongwanji describes intervening senses such as weariness, shrinking back, and ennui before having idle time. These sources support the traditional explanation and a proposed semantic account, but do not prove the historical path from the Buddhist usage to modern boredom. The accounts differ in how directly they present that development, without establishing a contradiction.

guides.explanation_en: 気にする means to care about, mind, or be concerned about something. 気 means one’s mind or attention, に marks what that attention is directed toward, and する expresses attending to it; together, the phrase describes taking something as a concern.

parts.contribution_en: One’s mind or attention, here the focus of concern.
Marks what the mind or attention is directed toward.
Expresses attending to that focus, forming the sense of caring about or minding it.

guides.explanation_en: する can mean doing an activity, or talking about and telling something with 話をする. In other common patterns, a sound is made or heard, a sensation or urge is felt, a sign is perceived, or someone has a particular expression or appearance; with a person, it can mean to engage with or treat them, and with an event, to happen. The words and grammatical pattern around する show which use applies.
聞く (きく) means to hear or listen to sounds, and to learn information by hearing it. It also means to ask or inquire, using a question to obtain information.
天秤棒 is a pole carried across the shoulders, with loads balanced at its ends. 天秤 contributes the balancing arrangement, and 棒 means “pole.”

parts.contribution_en: Balance or scale; here, the arrangement for balancing loads at the pole’s ends.
Pole.

guides.explanation_en: ということで frames what was just mentioned as a basis or point of association for what follows. Depending on the link, it can mean “with that in mind” or “speaking of that.”

parts.contribution_en: Presents the preceding statement or matter as the fact being taken up.
Marks that matter as the basis or circumstance connecting to what follows.

guides.explanation_en: 裏 (うら) means the back or rear side of something. It can also refer to the area behind it.
騒ぐ (さわぐ) means to make noise or behave rowdily. It describes this noisy, unruly behavior as a whole.
上手く is the く-form of 上手い, meaning “skilled” or “good at something.” With なる (“become”), it means to become skilled, often describing improvement in an ability.

parts.contribution_en: skilled or good at something; く-form of 上手い before なる
become, marking a change into that state

guides.explanation_en: 動かずに combines 動く (“move”) with ずに (“without doing”), and いる indicates that the resulting state continues. Together, 動かずにいる means “to remain without moving.”

parts.contribution_en: Means “without moving”: ずに marks not doing the action expressed by 動く.
Indicates continuing to be in that state.

guides.explanation_en: 立てる means to cause something to arise or be produced. It commonly describes producing a sound, as in 音を立てる (make a sound).
決心 means a firm decision or resolve to do something. 決 contributes making a decision, while 心 contributes the intention or resolve behind it; together they describe a settled intention to act.

parts.contribution_en: Contributes making a decision.
Contributes the intention or resolve behind the decision.

guides.explanation_en: 必ず marks an event or condition as occurring every time, without fail, or as certain to occur. It can describe a repeated pattern as well as a strong expectation or intention; the surrounding context determines which.

After a verb in the past form, ことはない says there has been no occasion when the action happened: the speaker has never done it. After a negative potential form, it denies that the inability exists, meaning “it’s not that one can’t”; this often presents the action as possible, sometimes with a qualified tone.

parts.contribution_en: Turns the preceding verb phrase into an experience or a state of being able or unable to act.
Marks that experience or state as the point being denied.
Denies that the experience occurred, or, after a negative potential form, denies the inability.

investigation_questions.question: How, if at all, did its group-related sense relate to the earlier plural use of わがはい?

guides.explanation_en: 吾輩 is a formal, literary first-person pronoun, traditionally masculine, meaning “I/me.” In the spelling, 吾 suggests “self” or “my/our,” and 輩 suggests companions or a group, together giving a cue of a self associated with a group. In Japanese usage, the pronoun had an earlier plural “we/us” use before its singular “I/me” use developed.
guides.caveat_en: These component glosses help explain the spelling, but their role in the word’s historical formation is not established.

parts.contribution_en: Suggests “self” or “my/our” as a spelling cue.
Suggests companions or a group as a spelling cue; this is not the whole word’s conventional meaning.

sources.title: 我が輩（読み）ワガハイ - コトバンク（デジタル大辞泉・精選版 日本国語大辞典）
sources.summary_en: Digital Daijisen describes わがはい as a masculine first-person pronoun and gives both a singular, self-important use and a plural use. The historical dictionary records a masculine plural use, with an example dated around 1467, then says the singular use developed from it, with an example dated 1871–72. Both dictionaries also separately list わがともがら, meaning ‘our companions/us’; this is a different reading from わがはい.

sources.title: 吾 | 漢字一字 - 漢字ペディア
sources.summary_en: The kanji reference gives 吾 the Japanese readings われ and わが, with senses including ‘self’ and ‘my/our.’ It lists 吾が as a word form. This supports a modern component gloss, not the historical derivation of 吾輩.

sources.title: 我が（読み）ワガ - コトバンク（デジタル大辞泉・精選版 日本国語大辞典）
sources.summary_en: Digital Daijisen defines わが as ‘mine/my’ or ‘ours/our’ and analyzes it as わ plus the particle が. The historical dictionary likewise analyzes わが as わ plus が, with historical examples. The page identifies 吾が as an alternate spelling.

sources.title: 輩（読み）トモガラ - コトバンク（デジタル大辞泉・精選版 日本国語大辞典）
sources.summary_en: The Japanese dictionary gives 輩, read ともがら, meanings such as companions and people of the same kind. Its kanji entry also gives the reading はい and the sense ‘companions of the same rank.’ These Japanese senses support a group-related component gloss.

claims.text_en: As a modern component gloss, 吾 can contribute ‘self’ or ‘my/our’: the kanji reference gives it the readings われ and わが and those senses, while the Japanese dictionary analyzes わが as わ plus が and defines it as ‘my/our.’ This supports a cautious component interpretation of the spelling 吾輩, but does not establish how the word historically formed.

輩 has Japanese group-related senses, including ‘companions’ and ‘people of the same kind.’ A gloss such as ‘my/our companions’ is therefore useful for explaining the written components, but it is not the conventional lexical meaning of わがはい.

The established Japanese word わがはい is a masculine first-person pronoun. The historical dictionary records an earlier plural use, ‘we/us,’ and describes the singular ‘I/me’ use as developing from it; its cited examples are dated around 1467 and 1871–72 respectively. This documents a Japanese usage history, not an etymological derivation from the modern meanings of 吾 and 輩.

The dictionary’s わがともがら entry means ‘our companions/us,’ but it is read ともがら, not はい. Its existence is consistent with the component gloss, but does not prove that わがはい historically arose from that phrase.
